rejected.title: Compound-complex sentences
card: A main clause makes sense on its own. A dependent clause adds extra detail but cannot stand alone. It often starts with a word like because, when, if or although.
A compound-complex sentence has at least two main clauses and at least one dependent clause.
Example: Because the rain was heavy, we stayed in, and we played cards. The main clauses are we stayed in and we played cards. The dependent clause is Because the rain was heavy.
This lets a writer give a reason or condition and carry on with a second idea, all in one sentence.
rejected.remember: Compound-complex means two or more main clauses plus a dependent clause.

a.q: Which sentence is a compound-complex sentence?
opts: When Zara arrived, the bus had left, so she walked home
Zara missed the bus, so she walked home
When Zara arrived, the bus had left
Zara walked home after she missed the bus
a.why: The first sentence has two main clauses (the bus had left, she walked home) and a dependent clause starting with when. The second is compound only, because it has no dependent clause. The third and fourth have only one main clause each.
a.clue: Look for two main clauses and one clause that cannot stand alone.

b.q: Which change turns "Leo trained hard, and he won the race" into a compound-complex sentence?
opts: Adding "because he wanted a medal" to the end
Replacing "and" with a full stop
Removing the word "and"
Adding "in the morning" to the end
b.why: The sentence already has two main clauses. Adding a dependent clause starting with because makes it compound-complex. Adding "in the morning" gives only extra detail, not a clause with its own verb, so the sentence stays compound.
b.clue: You need a new clause with its own verb that cannot stand alone.

version.title: Compound-complex sentences
card: A main clause has its own subject and verb and makes sense alone. A dependent clause has a verb but cannot stand alone, and often starts with because, when, if or although.
A compound-complex sentence has at least two main clauses and at least one dependent clause. Two verbs that share one subject, as in "Sam ran and hid", make one main clause.
Example: "If it stops raining, we will swim, and Dad will cook." The main clauses are "we will swim" and "Dad will cook". "If it stops raining" is the dependent clause.
This lets a writer add a reason or condition and carry an idea further, all in one sentence.
version.remember: Two or more main clauses plus a dependent clause make a compound-complex sentence.

opts: When the bell rang, Ali packed up, and Kim ran outside
When the bell rang, Ali packed up and left the classroom
Ali packed up his bag, and Kim ran outside to the oval
Ali packed up his bag when the bell rang at three
a.why: It has two main clauses, "Ali packed up" and "Kim ran outside", and the dependent clause "When the bell rang". The sentence about leaving the classroom has only one main clause, because Ali is the subject of both verbs.
a.clue: Count the subjects with their own verbs, then find a clause that cannot stand alone.

b.q: Mia wants to add a reason to "Mia studied, and she passed the test" and keep both main clauses. Which version is compound-complex?
opts: Mia studied because she was nervous, and she passed the test
Mia studied after school, and she passed the test on Monday
Mia was nervous, so she studied, and she passed the test
Because she was nervous, Mia studied hard for the maths test
b.why: "Because she was nervous" is a dependent clause, and both main clauses stay. In "Mia was nervous, so she studied", the reason is a main clause, so that sentence has three main clauses and no dependent clause.
b.clue: The reason must be a clause that cannot stand alone.
